query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (3–5 atomic percent) of a high-melting‐point refractory element (such as niobium) to the primary Ti–Ni high‐entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, solid‐solution high‐entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, produced by standard arc melting or similar processing and exhibiting a homogeneous FCC or BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 3–5 at.% niobium during alloy preparation (e.g., via arc melting and subsequent homogenization) without disrupting the single-phase solid solution.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under elevated temperatures (e.g., tensile and compressive tests between 600°C and 1200°C) in an inert or controlled atmosphere (to minimize oxidation) with the alloy compositions maintained near the equiatomic or near-equiatomic balance of Ti and Ni with the Nb addition.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of Nb is expected to be incorporated in the solid solution without changing the single-phase structure, thereby enhancing lattice distortion and improving grain boundary cohesion; this refined microstructure will inhibit dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
generation.mechanism: Niobium’s high melting point and strong solid-solution strengthening effect increase the resistance to thermally activated dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures. The enhanced lattice distortion from Nb leads to improved dislocation pinning, thus sustaining a higher yield strength and ductility under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-modified alloy will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and improved ductility (or reduced strain softening) at elevated temperatures relative to the base Ti–Ni alloy that lacks the Nb addition.
generation.baseline: The as-prepared titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy without any microalloying additions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for single-phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloys processed by conventional melting methods and tested in a controlled (inert or low-oxygen) environment at temperatures roughly between 600°C and 1200°C. Deviations in overall composition or processing conditions (e.g., oxidizing environments) may alter the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum Nb concentration and processing parameters need further optimization. There is uncertainty regarding long-term phase stability and cyclic thermal performance, and whether Nb may interact with any residual impurities to produce deleterious secondary phases under some conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one series of the baseline Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy and one series with 3–5 at.% Nb added during alloying. Perform identical homogenization treatments and verify, via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), that both retain a single-phase solid solution. Subject both groups to elevated-temperature mechanical tests (tensile and compressive) in a controlled inert atmosphere over the range of 600°C to 1200°C.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at each test temperature
Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase uniformity by XRD/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and/or ductility at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline, or if addition of Nb generates phase instability (e.g., appearance of secondary phases or precipitates), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
